item.title: [Logistics 101 #6] Every Dollar You Don't Spend Is a Dollar You Don't Have to Earn
item.body:
> Procurement is the discipline of deciding what to buy, who to buy it from, and how to keep that relationship working — and because purchased goods and services are the single largest line item in most companies, a dollar saved there lands on the profit line far faster than a dollar chased through sales.

## Today's Concept

Ask most people what a company does and they'll describe what it sells. But look at the income statement of almost any manufacturer, retailer, or restaurant group and you'll find the same thing: the biggest number isn't payroll or rent. It's what the company **bought** — raw materials, components, packaging, freight, contract services. In many manufacturing firms, purchased goods and services eat more than half of every sales dollar.

That's why procurement matters, and why it's the sixth stop in this series. Here are the four ideas that hold it together.

**1. Purchasing is a transaction. Procurement is a strategy.**
Purchasing is the narrow act of issuing a purchase order and paying the invoice. Procurement is the whole arc around it: figuring out what the business actually needs, deciding whether to make it in-house or buy it, finding and qualifying suppliers, negotiating terms, and managing performance for years afterward. Purchasing asks "what's the price?" Procurement asks "what's the **total cost of ownership**?"

```
Total Cost of Ownership = purchase price
                        + freight and duties
                        + inventory carrying cost
                        + inspection, scrap, and rework
                        + downtime and expediting
                        + switching or exit costs
```

A part that costs $9.20 instead of $10.00 is not cheaper if it fails inspection twice as often or ships from three weeks farther away.

**2. Not every purchase deserves the same effort.**
The standard tool here is the **Kraljic matrix**, which sorts everything you buy along two axes: how much money is involved, and how risky the supply is (few suppliers, fragile source, long lead time). That gives four quadrants, each with a different playbook:

- **Non-critical** (low spend, low risk) — office supplies, cleaning goods. Automate it. Use a catalog, a P-card, and stop thinking about it.
- **Leverage** (high spend, low risk) — commodity packaging, standard fasteners. Many capable suppliers want your volume. Compete them, consolidate volume, negotiate hard.
- **Bottleneck** (low spend, high risk) — a proprietary sensor, a single certified calibration lab. Small money, big pain if it stops. Hold safety stock, qualify a backup, sign a longer contract.
- **Strategic** (high spend, high risk) — the engine, the chip, the signature ingredient. Few alternatives, enormous impact. Build a genuine partnership, share forecasts, invest in the relationship.

The mistake almost every under-resourced team makes is spending its best people on the wrong quadrant — running competitive bids on paper towels while the sole-source component nobody has a backup for quietly becomes an existential risk.

**3. Make-or-buy is a strategic choice, not a spreadsheet.**
Outsourcing tends to win on cost, flexibility, and access to specialized capability. Keeping it in-house tends to win on control, quality assurance, IP protection, and responsiveness. The durable rule of thumb: **outsource what is not your core competency, and be extremely careful outsourcing anything a customer would notice.** The catch is that outsourcing doesn't remove risk — it converts execution risk into supplier risk. Boeing's 787 program is the textbook case: an aggressive outsourcing model spread design and fabrication across a deep global supplier tier, and the resulting integration and coordination problems contributed to years of delay.

**4. Contracts don't manage relationships. People do.**
**Supplier Relationship Management (SRM)** is the practice of segmenting suppliers, scoring them on real metrics, and investing management attention where it pays off. A typical scorecard runs on **QCDS** — quality (defect rate, PPM), cost (price trend, cost-reduction ideas), delivery (on-time-in-full percentage), and service (responsiveness, technical support). You cannot run a deep partnership with 4,000 suppliers, and you shouldn't try. You run transactional discipline with most of them, preferred-supplier terms with a couple hundred, and true joint development with the handful that determine whether your product is any good.

## In Everyday Life

Say you run **Trailhead Coffee**, a nine-location café chain in Austin. Annual revenue is $6.2 million, net margin about 5%, and roughly $2.4 million a year goes out the door to suppliers.

Your buying list sorts itself into the quadrants almost immediately.

**Green coffee beans — strategic.** Around $520,000 a year, and your entire brand rests on it. There is no interchangeable substitute; customers can taste a switch. So you don't run this on an annual bid. You sign a multi-year agreement with your Chiapas importer, visit the co-op, share your growth forecast so they can plan their crop, and accept that you'll pay a little more for consistency and first call on the good lots.

**Cups, lids, and sleeves — leverage.** About $310,000 a year, and a dozen distributors in Texas would love the business. This is where a competitive RFQ pays. You consolidate all nine stores onto one contract instead of letting each manager order locally, and you land 9% off — roughly $28,000.

**Espresso machine service — bottleneck.** Maybe $18,000 a year. Trivial money. But exactly one certified tech in the metro services your machines, and if a grouphead fails on a Saturday at your busiest store, you lose $2,800 in a day. So you pay for a service contract with a guaranteed four-hour response, and you keep a spare set of critical parts on the shelf. Small spend, deliberate attention.

**Office and cleaning supplies — non-critical.** Around $40,000. Put it on a punch-out catalog with one distributor, give managers a spending limit, and never hold a meeting about it again.

Now the part that makes the CFO sit up. That $28,000 saved on cups is $28,000 of pure operating profit. To generate the same $28,000 through sales at a 5% net margin, you'd have to sell **$560,000** more coffee — roughly a tenth of the entire business. That's the **profit-leverage effect**, and it's why procurement is one of the highest-return functions in a company that nobody outside the building ever thinks about.

The catch: chase that saving into the wrong quadrant — switch to a cheaper green coffee supplier to save $30,000 — and you may lose regulars who never tell you why they stopped coming. Savings that damage the product aren't savings.

## 3-Line Recap

1. Purchasing pays invoices; procurement decides what to buy, from whom, and on what terms — judged on total cost of ownership, not sticker price.
2. Segment your spend (Kraljic: non-critical, leverage, bottleneck, strategic) and match your effort to the quadrant, because uniform effort wastes it.
3. Outsourcing converts execution risk into supplier risk, so SRM — scorecards, segmentation, real relationships — is what keeps the savings from turning into an outage.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**1.** A component costs very little each year, but only one certified supplier in the world makes it and a stoppage would halt your line. In the Kraljic matrix, this is:
- (A) Non-critical
- (B) Leverage
- (C) Bottleneck
- (D) Strategic

**2.** True or False: A company with a 4% net profit margin that cuts $100,000 from its purchasing costs achieves the same profit impact as generating $100,000 in additional sales.

**3.** Which of these is the best description of Total Cost of Ownership?
- (A) The unit price plus sales tax
- (B) The purchase price plus all downstream costs of using that item, including freight, carrying cost, quality failures, and downtime
- (C) The total dollar value of all purchase orders issued in a year
- (D) The supplier's manufacturing cost plus their profit margin

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Procurement** — The end-to-end process of identifying needs, sourcing and qualifying suppliers, contracting, buying, and managing supplier performance.
- **Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)** — The full cost of acquiring and using a purchased item, including freight, inventory carrying, quality failures, downtime, and switching costs — not just the price.
- **Kraljic Matrix** — A spend-segmentation framework plotting purchases by financial impact and supply risk into four quadrants (non-critical, leverage, bottleneck, strategic), each with its own sourcing strategy.
- **Supplier Relationship Management (SRM)** — Segmenting the supply base and systematically managing performance and collaboration, concentrating attention on the suppliers that most affect the business.
- **Profit-Leverage Effect** — The principle that a dollar saved in purchasing raises operating profit by roughly a full dollar, while a dollar of new sales raises it only by the margin rate.

---

*Answers: **1 — (C) Bottleneck.** Low spend but high supply risk. The correct response isn't hard negotiation (there's no leverage at that volume) but risk mitigation: safety stock, a qualified second source, and a longer-term contract.*

***2 — False.** It's dramatically better. At a 4% margin, $100,000 in additional sales yields about $4,000 of profit, while $100,000 in purchasing savings drops close to the full $100,000 to the bottom line — you'd need roughly $2.5 million in new sales to match it. That's the profit-leverage effect.*

***3 — (B).** TCO captures everything the item costs you over its life, not just the invoice. It's the reason the lowest bid frequently loses on a properly built evaluation.*
